title: Senterej
summary: The chess of the Ethiopian highlands, a living descendant of the old shatranj: a short-stepping sew beside the negus, elephants that leap two squares diagonally, and kings that do not face each other across the board.
howToPlay: Move one piece per turn and capture by landing on an enemy piece; each piece has its own fixed way of moving.
Elephants (fil) leap exactly two squares on a diagonal, horses (ferese) leap like a chess knight, rooks (der) run along rows and columns.
Foot soldiers (medeq) step forward one square, capture diagonally forward and become a sew on the far edge.
Trap the opposing negus so it cannot escape attack to win.
rules: The back row reads der, ferese, fil, sew, negus, fil, ferese, der from the lower player; the opposing army is turned half a circle, so the two negus stand on different files.

The negus steps one square in any direction; the sew steps one square diagonally; the fil leaps two squares diagonally, over anything in between; the ferese leaps like a knight; the der moves any distance along a row or column.
Soldiers step one square forward, capture diagonally forward and become a sew when they reach the far row. There is no double step, no capture in passing and no castling.
A negus may never be left under attack; trapping it with no escape wins.
A player with no legal move who is not under attack draws.
The same position three times is a draw.
In the village game both sides first set up their armies freely without taking turns until the first capture; in this edition the sides move in turn from the start.
heritageNote: Senterej is played in Ethiopia and Eritrea, in cafes and under trees, and is the last widely played form of the medieval shatranj. Local custom varies on promotion, on how a lone king may be hunted and on the free opening phase, so this edition follows the common core.
